vignette:
He can still feel the water, even now, three years later. It isn’t a memory he chooses to visit; it arrives without warning—a cold rush up his calves, the smell of diesel and mud, the pressure of debris against his chest. He is a judge. He is supposed to be impartial, rational, the kind of man who weighs evidence without letting emotion tip the scale. But in the small hours of the morning, when his wife sleeps beside him, he is not a judge. He is a man pinned against a concrete pillar in a parking garage, watching the flood surge higher.

The event happened during the monsoon season in his home city, a coastal capital that had never seen anything like it. He had been driving back from a late hearing when the water rose so fast it swallowed the road. He abandoned his car, climbed three floors of a municipal garage with dozens of others. For fourteen hours, he clung to a railing as the current tugged at his legs. A child next to him slipped. He cannot remember if he reached for her. He remembers the sound—a high, thin cry that cut off. He told the rescue workers later that he did everything he could. He is no longer certain.

In the months afterward, he returned to work. The courthouse had been damaged, but the docket resumed. He sat on the bench, listened to testimony, delivered sentences. He found himself scanning the courtroom for exits. He began to notice the hum of the air conditioning—a sound that reminded him of the motor of a rescue boat. His hands would sweat. He started issuing rulings more quickly, cutting off cross-examination, needing to get the room empty. Lawyers noticed. One asked if he was ill. He said he was fine.

At home, he is not fine. He wakes at 2:47 a.m. every night—the time the child slipped—and lies still, heart hammering, listening to the rain. He has not told his wife. She asks why he flinches when she touches his back. He says he is tired. He avoids the news during monsoon season. He has stopped taking the coastal highway. He checks weather apps compulsively, sometimes twenty times a day, even when the sky is clear. If the forecast shows a 30 percent chance of rain, he cancels plans. He has begun to keep a change of clothes and a bottle of water in his car at all times. He knows this is irrational. He is a man who relies on logic. But logic does not stop the images: the brown water, the child’s face, the way the railing vibrated under the weight of people.

His most difficult moments come during cases involving negligence—a landlord who failed to maintain a drainage system, a contractor whose building collapsed after a storm. He recuses himself when he can. When he cannot, he forces himself to listen, but his pulse races. He feels the anger, hot and sharp, and he wonders if he is punishing the defendant or the memory. He is afraid he is becoming the kind of judge he once criticized: one who lets his history write the verdict.

He told his primary care doctor he was having trouble sleeping. The doctor prescribed a mild sedative. He takes it only on nights when the forecast says rain. This morning, his wife found him standing at the bedroom window at 4 a.m., staring at a puddle in the driveway. She asked what he was looking at. He said nothing. He is a judge. He is trained to find the truth. But the truth, he has learned, is not always something you can rule on. Sometimes it is just water, lapping at your feet, waiting for you to fall.
